messages.author: 3671e7fed9c01e6f
messages.subject: custom probabilities - normalization - slow
parts:
Hi,

I've recently started to try out Stan, after having speed problems with JAGS. Still, I run into the same with Stan, so I was wondering if there's someone out there who could point me in a direction how to speed up things - or tell me that my models are just not suitable for Stan.

I model time series as Markov processes. At each time step, the random variable y_t is a sample of a finite number of possible outcomes, say {1,...,M}. The probability mass function of y_t changes at each time step and is a function involving some standard density functions and a custom function based on covariates. Something like this
y_t | y_{t-1}  ~  some_density(y_t; y_{t-1}) * custom_function(y_t; covariates) / normalization_constant
The likelihood is the product of all those pieces for the entire time series.

The problem is the normalization constant. For each time step, it is the sum of the numerator evaluated for all possible outcomes {1,...,M}, and it involves the model parameters, so cannot just be ignored as a constant. This sum has to be calculated for each time step.

I run into the problem that if M (number of possible outcomes at each step) and N (number of time steps in time series) are large, say M=400, N=1000, calculating the normlization constant slows the sampling down a lot.

I was hoping that Stan would be better suited to this than JAGS, because it compiles a C++ code. If I do similar calculations (summing to obtain the normalization constants) just in C++, it is simple and fast. So I am wondering whether the implementation of summing is somehow time consuming in Stan, or whether it's the calculation of gradients, or something else.

I'd be very grateful if someone would comment on this. Any help and info is appreciated.

I've made a little fake example of the model type that I'm trying to fit that has the speed problems. I am attaching 2 versions of stan model formulations that I tried. "fakeCustom.stan" uses increment_log_prob() to manually specify the log-likelihood. "fakeCategorial.stan" uses a categorical distribution for each y_t - using categorical_logit to normalize the probabilities. I also tried categorical in combination with softmax(), but that didn't improve things.
I am also attaching R dump files with fake data for both stan models. For this data, I used M=50 and N=100. This is much lower than what I really need, but this is more suitable for demonstration (because possible to run). After compiling the model, running just 100 iterations takes a few minutes with both model versions. For M=few hundred, N=1000, it would take much longer.
It tried both using Stan via command line and rstan. For rstan, I also attach files that are capable of producing the fake data and fit the models via stan().

On Feb 21, 2014, at 5:26 PM, Ulrike Schlägel <ulrike.s...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I've recently started to try out Stan, after having speed problems with JAGS. Still, I run into the same with Stan, so I was wondering if there's someone out there who could point me in a direction how to speed up things - or tell me that my models are just not suitable for Stan.
>
> I model time series as Markov processes. At each time step, the random variable y_t is a sample of a finite number of possible outcomes, say {1,...,M}. The probability mass function of y_t changes at each time step and is a function involving some standard density functions and a custom function based on covariates. Something like this
> y_t | y_{t-1} ~ some_density(y_t; y_{t-1}) * custom_function(y_t; covariates) / normalization_constant
> The likelihood is the product of all those pieces for the entire time series.
>
> The problem is the normalization constant. For each time step, it is the sum of the numerator evaluated for all possible outcomes {1,...,M}, and it involves the model parameters, so cannot just be ignored as a constant. This sum has to be calculated for each time step.
>
> I run into the problem that if M (number of possible outcomes at each step) and N (number of time steps in time series) are large, say M=400, N=1000, calculating the normlization constant slows the sampling down a lot.
>
> I was hoping that Stan would be better suited to this than JAGS, because it compiles a C++ code. If I do similar calculations (summing to obtain the normalization constants) just in C++, it is simple and fast. So I am wondering whether the implementation of summing is somehow time consuming in Stan, or whether it's the calculation of gradients, or something else.

Yes, it's the gradients that slow down the sum. Calculating sums in Stan is just as
fast as in C++ -- it just reduces to the obvious C++ analogue. But calculating
gradients builds up the whole expression tree in memory for the sum then propagates
derivatives backward with the chain rule in a second pass.

But this might not be why sampling is slow.

When you say it's fast in C++, you mean you have a sampler written in C++ that
gets good effective sample sizes per second? If so, what sampling algorithm are
you using?

> I'd be very grateful if someone would comment on this. Any help and info is appreciated.
>
> I've made a little fake example of the model type that I'm trying to fit that has the speed problems. I am attaching 2 versions of stan model formulations that I tried. "fakeCustom.stan" uses increment_log_prob() to manually specify the log-likelihood. "fakeCategorial.stan" uses a categorical distribution for each y_t - using categorical_logit to normalize the probabilities. I also tried categorical in combination with softmax(), but that didn't improve things.
> I am also attaching R dump files with fake data for both stan models. For this data, I used M=50 and N=100. This is much lower than what I really need, but this is more suitable for demonstration (because possible to run). After compiling the model, running just 100 iterations takes a few minutes with both model versions. For M=few hundred, N=1000, it would take much longer.
> It tried both using Stan via command line and rstan. For rstan, I also attach files that are capable of producing the fake data and fit the models via stan().

Looking at your fakeCustom file, you can define

log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(...)

and use that rather than log(weight[n]) because

log_inv_logit(u) =def= log(inv_logit(u))

with

inv_logit(u) =def= 1 / (1 + exp(-u))

There is also a much faster and more arithmetically stable
function

log_sum_exp(v) = log(sum(exp(v))

So this:

for (i in 1:M)
normpiece[i] <- exp(-square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]));
norm <- sum(normpiece);

... log(norm) ...

can be replaced with

for (i in 1:M)
log_normpiece[i] <- -square(x[i]-y[n-1])/(2*square(sigma))) / (1+exp(-alpha-beta1*res1[n,i]-beta2*res2[n,i]);
log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);

... log_norm ...

where again the 1/(1 + exp(-u)) bit can be replaced with inv_logit(u).

So your two blocks would look something like:

transformed parameters {
real<lower=0, upper=1> log_weight[N];
for (n in 1:N)
log_weight[n] <- log_inv_logit(-alpha - beta1 * cov1[n] - beta2 * cov2[n]);
}
model {
real log_norm;
real square_sigma;
vector[M] log_normpiece;
square_sigma <- square(sigma);
for (n in 2:N) {
for (i in 1:M)
normpiece[i]
<- -square(x[i] - y[n-1]) / (2*square(sigma))
+ log_inv_logit(alpha - beta1 * res1[n,i]- beta2 * res2[n,i]);
log_norm <- log_sum_exp(log_normpiece);
increment_log_prob( (-0.5) * square(y[n] - y[n-1]) / square_sigma
+ log_weight[n] - log_norm );
}
}

You should check my algebra here --- you had lots of brackets floating around.
Note that I also changed - u / 2 to (- 0.5) * u, which replaces a negation and
division with a single multiplication.

All of this will only make the iterations faster --- it won't help at
all with effective sample size if that's your issue.

Is it sampling properly, just slowly?

You don't need to go back to Stan 2.1.0 --- the issue was with Rcpp.
But we've worked around the install issues for that, too. Not that
it'll make any difference for this problem.

- Bob

Hi Bob,

Thank you very much for looking at my problem and suggesting more efficient formulations!

I've tried out your suggestions, and using the log_sum_exp() instead of a straightforward sum did make the sampling a little bit faster. Still, I ran a test with higher dimensions and sample size (time series length N=1000, number of possible outcomes of each step M=225), and a run with 100 iterations took 1.5 hours. So it seems to me that just the sampling is already slow, without even thinking yet about effective sample size.

So HMC is maybe not the best method for my model type?

Thanks a lot again for taking the time to look at my model and your help.

Uli

Do other samplers run faster and get the right answer?

If you get 20 or 30 effective samples with 100 iterations,
that may be all you need --- it's all you need for most MCMC
inference.

- Bob
